[TODAY] Some giant stars may die without exploding. 💫

A Caltech-led team studied 257 black hole mergers heard by gravitational-wave detectors: three in four involve black holes about 10 times the Sun's mass. Black holes of 12 to 16 Sun masses turned out to be unusually rare.

That pattern matches a prediction for failed supernovae, where a massive star collapses inward instead of blowing apart.

Reality check: this is a strong hint, not proof. No failed supernova has been directly confirmed yet.

[TODAY] Mars rover leftovers are heading to the Moon. 🌙

On Nov. 7, NASA said it is moving ahead with PROMISE, a six-wheeled, nuclear-powered rover for the Moon's south pole. JPL is building it from spare flight parts and test models of the Curiosity and Perseverance Mars rovers, which saves time and money.

Its job: drill about 3 feet (1 m) down, look for ice and help choose sites for a future Moon base. Nuclear power lets it work through long lunar nights and inside craters the Sun never lights.

Reality check: launch is targeted for late 2028, for an 18-month mission.

[TODAY] Why does Mercury take eight years to reach? ☀️

Earth is on average ten times closer to Mercury than to Jupiter, yet the trips take similar time. The reason: as a spacecraft falls toward the Sun, it speeds up like a car rolling downhill. Arrive too fast and Mercury's gravity can't catch you.

So the ESA and JAXA mission BepiColombo braked the slow way: nine planet flybys (Earth once, Venus twice, Mercury six times) over 9.9 billion km since 2018.

Reality check: orbit entry is scheduled for Nov. 21; science starts in April 2027.

Save this for the next "why so slow?" question.

[TODAY] The planet was in the picture all along. 🔭

Stars outshine their planets so badly that planets vanish in the glare. A team from Northwestern, Caltech, MIT and STScI built a digital twin of the James Webb Space Telescope's infrared camera, modeled millions of tiny optical flaws, then subtracted the star's light.

On known planets, it was 2 to 15 times more sensitive than standard methods. In one Webb image where the usual processing missed the planet 51 Eri b, it showed up clearly. The study appeared in Nature on Nov. 4.

Reality check: 51 Eri b was already known. The prize is old Webb data that may hide new worlds.

[IMAGINE] Rack-sized computers are booked for orbit in 2029. 🛰️

What is real: on Nov. 19, Google said a New Glenn rocket will launch its Project Suncatcher satellites in early 2029. Each satellite will carry about one data center rack of computing. A prototype has been in orbit since Oct. 1, testing the chips against radiation and heat.

Reality check: these are company plans for a long-term research project. The claim of up to eight times more solar power in orbit is Google's.

The speculation: what if your AI answers one day came from sun-powered computers in orbit?
